The 1-month estimate continues that gradual drift upward to 97, which represents roughly a 2–3% gain over the period — a fairly conservative assumption of trend continuation without assuming any dramatic catalyst in either direction.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard volatility scaling across time horizons. For the 1-day interval, the roughly ±2.6-point range captures typical daily fluctuations under normal market conditions, implying an annualized volatility assumption in the moderate range. As the horizon extends to one week, the interval widens to ±6 points, and by one month it expands to ±14 points, consistent with volatility scaling proportional to the square root of time. These widths also incorporate some additional uncertainty beyond pure statistical volatility — namely, that forecasting accuracy degrades meaningfully as the horizon lengthens and more unknown information can arrive.

On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical shock could drive sharp selling pressure that breaks below the lower bound of any horizon. Liquidity events or correlated asset selloffs — particularly in risk-off environments — tend to be fat-tailed and would not be fully captured by a symmetric confidence interval. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic release, a surprise dovish pivot by a major central bank, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push the asset well above the upper bounds, especially at the 1-month horizon where there is more time for compounding positive surprises.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates are constructed under significant epistemic uncertainty. I don't have real-time market data, so my baseline level and current trend assumptions could themselves be off. The intervals are best interpreted as rough probabilistic guides rather than precise quantitative outputs, and tail risks — particularly clustered volatility events — are systematically underrepresented in symmetric interval forecasts like this one.
